clue.text: Shock bastard with such a detailed account?

definitions.note: the answer is the adjective describing an account of this kind, one that leaves out no step

parts.note: a shock is a sudden setback, as in 'the news came as a blow'
by-blow is an old word for an illegitimate child

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether to stun a scoundrel by recounting every last detail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bastard' is not an insult or an anagram signal here: it is the old noun for a child born out of wedlock, which the dictionary also calls a by-blow.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: a report giving every successive incident in order is described with this hyphenated adjective, borrowed from boxing commentary.

clue.text: Polish expert in short comic role

definitions.meaning: as a verb, to shine a surface by rubbing it
an enthusiast who knows a subject well, as in a film or wine devotee

indicators.note: short means the word for the comic role loses its last letter

parts.note: a buffo is a comic part, or the singer of one, in Italian opera

explanation.surface: A specialist from Poland takes a small funny part on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: Three routes to one word: two definitions, then 'short' trims the last letter from BUFFO, opera's comic part. 'Polish' looks like the nationality but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Two dictionary synonyms: to shine something by rubbing, and a knowledgeable enthusiast.

clue.text: Welshman has nothing recent to bring up

parts.note: O looks like zero, nothing

indicators.note: in a down clue, bringing a word up means writing it from bottom to top

parts.note: something recent is new

explanation.surface: A man from Wales has no fresh topic to raise in conversation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to bring up' turns NEW into WEN in this down entry; 'has' simply joins definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a traditional Welsh forename and surname, as in the poet Wilfred or footballer Michael.

clue.text: Does one live precariously on it, in Lent weeks?

definitions.text: Does one live precariously on it

parts.note: lent as the past participle of lend: what is lent to you is what you have borrowed
weeks are a stretch of time

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether fasting through the weeks before Easter is a risky way to live.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital on 'Lent' suggests the church season, but it is just the past participle of lend. The definition is the question about what one lives on precariously.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: to live on this is to survive past the point when disaster was expected.

clue.text: Papers support British swimmer

indicators.note: in a down clue, the piece that supports another sits underneath it

parts.note: a ream is a quantity of sheets of paper, 500 of them

explanation.surface: The newspapers get behind a British athlete in the pool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'support' places REAM under B in this down entry. 'swimmer' is the crossword habit of calling a fish by what it does.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a freshwater or sea fish, and any fish can be called a swimmer in crosswords.

clue.text: What experts know related in paper

parts.note: from the British idiom 'to know one's onions', meaning to be expert in a subject
kin as an adjective means related by family, as in 'he is kin to me'

explanation.surface: Specialist knowledge is set out in an academic article.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To know one's onions' is a British idiom for being thoroughly expert, so what experts know is ONIONS. 'in' links wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a very thin, light, translucent kind of writing sheet once used for airmail.

clue.text: First to smack face showing such an irritating expression

indicators.note: first to tells us to take the opening letter of the next word

parts.note: mug is slang for the face

explanation.surface: Whoever lands the first slap on a face wears an annoying look.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: self-satisfied, which is how a person looks when wearing an annoyingly pleased-with-oneself grin.

clue.text: Maybe forty or fifty liable to spread?

definitions.text: Maybe forty or fifty liable to spread?

parts.words: Maybe forty or fifty liable to spread?
parts.note: people in their forties and fifties are said to thicken round the waist, a weight gain named after that time of life

explanation.definitionFit: Example plus idiom: forty or fifty is that stage of life, and the 'spread' is the proverbial waistline gain that comes with it.

clue.text: Knowing one's courses, but got masonry wrong

indicators.note: wrong says the letters of the two words before it are out of order and must be put right

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A student knows the syllabus well but makes a mess of the stonework module.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrong' rearranges GOT MASONRY. The 'courses' look like college classes, or layers of bricks, but they are the courses of a meal.
explanation.definitionFit: Whimsical description: the art and science of good eating, so expertise in the dishes of a meal.

clue.text: Charge duellers, if wounded

indicators.note: wounded means damaged, so the letters of the neighbouring words are broken up and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An order to rush at the men fighting a duel should they be hurt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wounded' rearranges DUELLERS IF. A charge in heraldry is any device borne on a shield, so 'Charge' is a noun here, not a command.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: the stylised lily is a heraldic device, and any such device on a shield is called a charge.

clue.text: Horace's work in Ukrainian port lacking appeal

indicators.note: lacking tells us the port's name goes without the letters for appeal

parts.note: Odessa is a major Ukrainian port on the Black Sea
SA is the old abbreviation for sex appeal

explanation.surface: A man called Horace toils in an unattractive Black Sea harbour town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lacking' removes SA, crosswords' old abbreviation for sex appeal, from ODESSA. 'in' links definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: the Roman poet's best-known collection of lyric poems bears this title.

clue.text: Final decision made about the Sistine wall?

parts.note: the final one is the last one
a decision, especially a court's, is a judgment

explanation.surface: The Vatican settles once and for all what to do with a chapel wall.
explanation.walkthrough: Michelangelo's huge fresco covers the altar wall of the Sistine Chapel, so the answer is, whimsically, what was 'made about' that wall.
explanation.definitionFit: Allusion: Michelangelo's fresco of this name fills the altar end of the Sistine Chapel.

clue.text: Author's poster on William the Conqueror, for one

indicators.note: in an across clue, one piece on another conventionally follows it

parts.note: William the Conqueror was Duke of Normandy, so he is an example of a Norman
someone who posts letters is a mailer

explanation.surface: A writer has a wall poster about the king who invaded England in 1066.
explanation.walkthrough: The poster is not a wall picture but someone who puts letters in the post; 'on' sets that piece second, the usual convention in an across clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: the American novelist who wrote The Naked and the Dead.

clue.text: Fancied heading off from one New World country into another shortly

indicators.note: into tells us the first trimmed country goes inside the second
shortly means the second country's name is cut short by its last letter

parts.note: another New World country: Chile, in South America

indicators.note: heading off from means the first country's name loses its opening letter

parts.note: America, the United States, is a country of the New World

explanation.surface: Someone liked the idea of leaving one American nation and soon entering a second.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancied' means imagined, not desired. 'heading off from' and 'shortly' each cost a country one letter, at the front and the back respectively, before 'into' nests the results.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: imaginary or fanciful, existing only as a product of the imagination.

clue.text: Apparently miserable Don Juan causing needless alarm

parts.note: someone in tears appears to be miserable
a Don Juan is a womaniser, and wolf is slang for a predatory seducer

explanation.surface: A visibly unhappy seducer is frightening people for no reason.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom from Aesop's fable of the shepherd boy: raising false alerts until nobody believes you.

clue.text: Murder, for example, cryptically, up here

parts.note: murder spelt in the other direction is Red Rum, Britain's famous Grand National winner, so the word is an example of a racing steed once turned round
cryptically asks us to describe what has been done to that steed's name to give the word murder: it has been written back to front, back

explanation.surface: A killing, say, is mysteriously committed somewhere upstairs.
explanation.walkthrough: A clue in reverse: 'Murder' is RED RUM written right to left, and Red Rum was Britain's famous racehorse, three times Grand National winner. 'cryptically' asks how a setter would clue 'murder'.
explanation.definitionFit: Location: where a rider sits, mounted up on a steed.

clue.text: Government opponent caught in rain -— hat's ruined

indicators.note: in tells us the letter for caught sits inside the rearranged letters
ruined means spoiled, so the letters of rain and hat's are broken up and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, the s included
C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A political dissident gets soaked in a downpour and his headgear is spoiled.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash hides that 'ruined' governs the words on both sides of it, giving ANARHIST; 'in' then admits the cricket scorecard's letter for caught.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: one who rejects all rule by the state.

clue.text: Mark the Finnish author?

parts.note: Finnish here means 'of Finn', that is Huckleberry Finn, whose author wrote under the first name Mark

explanation.definitionFit: Allusion: the pen name of Samuel Clemens, who wrote The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn.

clue.text: A few weeks in Bordeaux: time to get lubricated …

parts.note: a few weeks make a month, and in a French city such as Bordeaux a month is 'mois'

explanation.surface: A short holiday in French wine country is a chance to get well oiled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in Bordeaux' asks for the French word. 'to get' links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Near-synonym: slightly wet, as a surface is once oil or fluid has been applied.

clue.text: … until one's sick of a foreign language

definitions.text: … until one's sick of a foreign language

parts.words: … until one's sick of a foreign language
parts.note: a phrase meaning 'to the point of sickness', which belongs to a foreign language, Latin

explanation.definitionFit: Translation: the Latin tag used in English for something repeated to a sickening, tiresome degree.

clue.text: Excuse for war: government has a little money

parts.note: a regime is a government, especially an authoritarian one
change is small coins, a little money

explanation.surface: The state's pretext for fighting is that it is short of cash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has' joins the two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: replacing another country's rulers is a stated justification for invading it.

clue.text: Fish nibbling top off seaweed

indicators.note: nibbling the top off means the first letter, the top in a down entry, is bitten away

parts.note: tangle is a coarse brown seaweed, a kind of kelp

explanation.surface: A fish bites the tip off a frond of seaweed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nibbling top off' removes the T from TANGLE. 'Fish' is the verb, not the creature.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym as a verb: to try to catch fish with rod and line.

clue.text: Old woman finally changed internet access

indicators.note: finally changed means the last letter of the word is swapped for a different one

parts.note: 'old woman' is slang for one's wife

explanation.surface: An elderly lady at last switches her broadband provider.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finally changed' swaps the last letter of WIFE, E, for I; the clue does not say which letter replaces it, so the definition decides.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: the wireless networking technology by which most devices get online.

clue.text: Dish out main course, say

indicators.note: say tells us the word for the main course is spoken, not written

parts.note: the meat is the main dish of a traditional meal, as in 'meat and two veg'

explanation.surface: A host serves up the main part of the meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' makes MEAT, heard, into its soundalike. 'Dish out' is the definition, not part of the dinner.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: to distribute or allot, usually followed by 'out', as with punishment.

clue.text: Produce whip

definitions.meaning: as a noun, what a farm yields in a season
a short riding whip carried by a horse rider

explanation.definitionFit: Two noun senses: a harvest of farm yield, and a rider's short whip.

clue.text: Progress so narrowly, data being rather short?

definitions.meaning: to move forward one behind another in a line one person wide
whimsically, a store of data amounting to just one computer document is rather scanty

explanation.definitionFit: A literal sense and a whimsical one: walking one behind another, and a lone computer document's worth of information.

clue.text: Steal a ride

definitions.meaning: slang for to pilfer, as in shoplifting
a free journey in someone else's car, as a hitch-hiker gets

explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: slang for pilfering, and a free trip in another person's vehicle.

clue.text: With wire, bashes tsetse fly

indicators.note: bashes means knocks about, so the letters of wire and tsetse are battered into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone swats an African biting insect using a length of wire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bashes' rearranges WIRE TSETSE. 'fly' is not the insect but British slang for sharp and knowing; 'With' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: fly is British slang for shrewd and worldly, wise to the ways of city life.
